activities.prompt: What is the main point of the passage?
activities.passage: A small town replaced several car journeys with a shared electric shuttle. The service is not a complete solution, but it has connected older residents with shops and clinics.

options.text: A limited transport scheme has produced useful social benefits.
The town has removed every private car.
Older residents no longer need clinics.
The shuttle service is cheaper than every alternative.

activities.explanation: The passage balances a limitation with the practical connections the shuttle provides.

activities.prompt: Which detail is explicitly stated?
activities.passage: The museum's digital catalogue was launched in April. Curators added photographs gradually because many older records had to be checked first.

options.text: The catalogue launched in April.
Every record was already digital.
The photographs were taken by visitors.
The museum closed in April.

activities.explanation: The launch month is directly stated; the other options contradict or add unsupported information.

activities.prompt: What can be inferred about the volunteers?
activities.passage: The volunteers arrived before sunrise, divided the tasks without being asked and stayed until the final boxes were labelled.

options.text: They were organised and committed.
They were paid by the council.
They had never met before.
They disliked labelling boxes.

activities.explanation: Their early arrival, initiative and persistence support the inference of commitment and organisation.

activities.prompt: Why did the researchers repeat the test?
activities.passage: The first results looked promising, but the sample was small. The researchers repeated the test with more participants before making a public claim.

options.text: To make the evidence more reliable.
To reduce the number of participants.
To hide the first results.
To change the research question.

activities.explanation: Repeating the test with a larger sample addresses the weakness of the first result.

activities.prompt: Which summary is accurate?
activities.passage: The library introduced self-service returns. Staff were not removed; instead, they spent more time helping visitors find specialist material.

options.text: Automation changed staff duties rather than eliminating staff.
Visitors can no longer speak to staff.
Specialist material was removed.
The library stopped accepting returns.

activities.explanation: The passage explicitly contrasts changed duties with staff removal.

activities.prompt: What is the safest inference from the report?
activities.passage: The rooftop garden reduced the building's summer temperature slightly. The organisers are now monitoring water use before extending the project.

options.text: The project shows promise but needs further evidence.
The building no longer needs cooling.
Water use has already fallen dramatically.
The organisers will extend it immediately.

activities.explanation: A small benefit and continued monitoring justify a cautious conclusion.

activities.prompt: What does the second paragraph contribute?
activities.passage: The project began with a single repair workshop. It later trained residents to fix appliances at home, which reduced the number of items sent to landfill.

options.text: It explains how the project's impact expanded.
It proves every appliance can be repaired.
It describes a separate landfill scheme.
It shows that the workshop closed.

activities.explanation: Training residents extends the original workshop's effect and connects it to less landfill waste.

activities.prompt: Which claim is not supported?
activities.passage: The course attracted more applicants after its evening option was introduced. Attendance was steady, although the organisers did not measure completion rates.

options.text: The evening option attracted interest.
Attendance remained steady.
The course had a higher completion rate.
The organisers lacked one measure.

activities.explanation: The passage mentions applicants and attendance but gives no completion-rate comparison.

activities.prompt: Why is the conclusion deliberately limited?
activities.passage: The survey suggests that commuters value reliable buses, but it was conducted during one unusually cold week. The authors recommend a longer study.

options.text: The conditions may not represent normal travel.
Commuters never use buses in winter.
The survey had no answers.
Reliable buses are unpopular.

activities.explanation: An unusual week may affect responses, so the authors want broader evidence.

activities.prompt: What is the article mainly evaluating?
activities.passage: The article compares two ways of reducing food waste in schools. One is cheaper, while the other reaches more pupils and provides clearer data.

options.text: Trade-offs between two school strategies.
The history of school lunches.
The price of supermarket food.
A single successful recipe.

activities.explanation: The article weighs cost against reach and data quality rather than simply describing one method.

activities.prompt: What can be inferred about the archive team?
activities.passage: The archive postponed its digital launch after discovering that several labels used inconsistent dates. The team chose accuracy over a quick release.

options.text: They are willing to delay publication to improve reliability.
They have abandoned digitisation.
They prefer inaccurate records.
They have finished checking every label.

activities.explanation: The delay caused by inconsistent labels indicates a priority for accuracy.

activities.prompt: Which detail explains the project's limited reach?
activities.passage: The mentoring scheme received enthusiastic feedback, but it operated in only two neighbourhoods and relied on a small pool of mentors.

options.text: It had a restricted geographical and human capacity.
Participants gave no feedback.
It operated in every neighbourhood.
It had more mentors than required.

activities.explanation: Two neighbourhoods and few mentors explain why the positive results cannot be generalised widely.

activities.prompt: What is the author's central inference?
activities.passage: Employees used the quiet room most often before difficult meetings, while ordinary tasks were usually completed at shared desks. This suggests that the room functions as a preparation space rather than a general office.

options.text: Its value is linked to concentrated preparation.
Employees dislike shared desks.
Difficult meetings never happen at desks.
The room is used only by managers.

activities.explanation: The contrast in usage supports the conclusion about preparation and concentration.

activities.prompt: Which interpretation best fits the figures?
activities.passage: After the library extended opening hours, visits rose by 8 percent, but the increase was concentrated among students. Older visitors came at the same rate as before.

options.text: The change benefited one group more than another.
Every group visited more often.
Students stopped using the library.
Older visitors opposed the extension.

activities.explanation: The increase is real but concentrated among students; no opposition by older visitors is stated.

activities.prompt: Why does the writer mention the failed pilot?
activities.passage: The first pilot failed because residents were not told how the new system worked. The revised version began with demonstrations, after which participation improved.

options.text: To show how communication affected participation.
To prove the system can never work.
To explain why demonstrations were cancelled.
To compare two unrelated towns.

activities.explanation: The contrast between the two pilots connects explanation with improved participation.

activities.prompt: Which conclusion is justified by the evidence?
activities.passage: The roof panels produced less energy in winter, yet the building's annual electricity bill still fell. The report attributes the fall to improved insulation as well as the panels.

options.text: The reduction had more than one contributing cause.
The panels produced most energy in winter.
Insulation increased the bill.
The building stopped using electricity.

activities.explanation: The report explicitly attributes the fall to insulation and panels together.

activities.prompt: What is the article's main caution?
activities.passage: The app's users reported saving time, but the study measured self-reported estimates rather than actual task duration. The authors call for an independent trial.

options.text: The reported benefit has not yet been measured objectively.
Users reported no benefit.
The app cannot be tested.
Independent trials are unnecessary.

activities.explanation: Self-reported estimates leave the actual size of the benefit uncertain.

activities.prompt: Which statement best captures the two paragraphs?
activities.passage: The first paragraph describes a decline in local shops. The second explains that a new weekly market has brought some customers back, although it cannot replace daily trade.

options.text: A partial recovery is helping but does not solve the wider problem.
The market has replaced every shop.
Local trade has returned completely.
The market caused the original decline.

activities.explanation: The text presents an improvement while explicitly limiting its reach.

activities.prompt: What can be inferred about the policy?
activities.passage: The policy increased recycling in offices with clear collection points. In buildings where bins were hidden, the effect was negligible.

options.text: Implementation conditions influenced its success.
The policy worked equally everywhere.
Hidden bins increased recycling.
Offices had no collection points.

activities.explanation: The contrast between visible and hidden collection points shows that implementation mattered.

activities.prompt: Why is the author's conclusion qualified?
activities.passage: The mentoring trial improved attendance among participants who completed the first month. The report does not know whether the most frequently absent students joined the trial.

options.text: The participants may not represent the absent students.
Attendance fell among all participants.
The trial included every student.
The first month was never completed.

activities.explanation: Without knowing who joined, the improvement cannot be generalised to the most absent students.

activities.prompt: Which inference follows from the final sentence?
activities.passage: The council published the raw survey responses alongside its summary. This allowed residents to check whether the conclusions reflected the original answers.

options.text: The council wanted the process to be transparent.
Residents were forbidden to question the summary.
The raw responses were destroyed.
The survey had no conclusions.

activities.explanation: Publishing raw responses enables checking and therefore supports an inference of transparency.

activities.prompt: What is the strongest overall summary?
activities.passage: A university introduced shorter meetings, shared agendas in advance and recorded decisions. Staff reported less repetition, although some discussions needed more time.

options.text: A structured reform improved efficiency but created a small trade-off.
Meetings became shorter because discussion stopped.
Staff rejected all structure.
Recording decisions increased repetition.

activities.explanation: The summary combines the three changes, the benefit and the limitation.

activities.prompt: Which option overstates the evidence?
activities.passage: The new timetable reduced delays on two routes during the first month. The transport team plans to monitor other routes before recommending a wider change.

options.text: The timetable has solved delays across the network.
Two routes showed fewer delays.
The result is preliminary.
Other routes still need monitoring.

activities.explanation: The evidence covers two routes and one month, so a network-wide claim is too strong.

activities.prompt: What does the comparison imply?
activities.passage: The first design was cheaper to build, while the second used more durable materials. The committee selected the second after considering maintenance over ten years.

options.text: Long-term maintenance outweighed the initial saving.
The first design was more durable.
The committee ignored future costs.
Both designs cost the same to build.

activities.explanation: The selection after a ten-year maintenance review implies that durability mattered more than the initial price.

activities.prompt: What is the most defensible conclusion?
activities.passage: The pilot attracted strong interest but required more staff time than predicted. The organisers will keep it running while redesigning the registration process.

options.text: Interest is high, but the process is not yet efficient.
The pilot has failed completely.
The organisers will cancel it immediately.
Registration requires no staff.

activities.explanation: The organisers' decision shows value in the interest alongside a process problem.
